rv.q: That this is a major work won't surprise anyone who loved it at Theater's Off-Broadway space last winter. Recast for Broadway with two new actors, the five-character family drama feels even more powerful -- a boldly conventional yet altogether gripping work that knows individual psychology as keenly as it understands the world around it.

Jon Robin Baitz has written a family drama that crackles with the electricity of old wounds being picked at until they bleed afresh. This is a smart, savage and ultimately moving portrait of a family whose love for one another is both their salvation and their curse.
Baitz is back now in theater’s embrace with “Other Desert Cities,” a crackling new serio-comedy that affirms his place as a leader of the dramatic pack.

With humor, sensitivity and invigorating anger, Baitz is doing here what he set out to do in Brothers & Sisters as originally conceived, which is to examine the fractiousness of American politics through the prism of one family.
The script crackles with life and so do the performances.
He just makes spending time with these messed-up, complicated people a genuine pleasure.
Jon Robin Baitz has written a play that is both deeply personal and utterly theatrical.

The expert cast, under Joe Mantello's thoughtful direction, mines the resulting conflicts for all their hilarity and poignance. After Brooke pours her heart out defending her book, Thomas Sadoski's witty Trip offers an equally passionate (and entertaining) summation of the selfishness in her suffering and healing.
The Wyeths emerge as an all-American family, acting out against each other out of both love and self-interest.
Jon Robin Baitz has given them a terrific, insightful and often funny play, and they know just what to do with it.

Under Mantello's directional finesse, this exceptional five-member cast turns Baitz's blueprint of family squabbling into a portrait of regret and denial that is as witty and entertaining as it is emotionally cathartic.
Together, the five performers comprise what is no doubt the finest ensemble cast currently treading the boards in New York.
This astutely drawn and deliciously performed play is as juicy and surprising as ever.
The one thing that comes across with great power in both productions of this play for grown-ups is the sense of a dilemma that few of us can escape
Even as skilled a director (and frequent Baitz collaborator) as Joe Mantello can't keep the thing from sinking in implausibility.

cn.t: Baitz's explosive family drama earns strong praise for its crackling script and stellar performances, particularly Rachel Griffiths' knockout Broadway debut. Critics find the domestic showdown smart, riveting, and surprisingly fresh despite familiar territory.

vs.sum: The Booth Theatre offers good sightlines with a well-raked mezzanine and clear views from most seats, though legroom can be tight. The theater's elegant, European-inspired design adds to its charm, while sound quality is consistently praised. Facilities are average, with typical restroom and concession offerings.

acc.note: 6 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. Not completely wheelchair accessible. Infrared devices available.
